_comment: Security anti-patterns in this repository's own source that are ACCEPTED, each with the
reason -- and, for a TLS-verification skip, the set of hosts that client can reach.
scripts/check_security_footguns.py fails on any finding not listed here, and equally on any
entry here whose site has gone away or been FIXED: a closed gap left recorded goes on
excusing the file, and would silently re-cover the shape if it came back.
WHY A LEDGER AND NOT A BAN. fabric-emulator is deliberately insecure in documented ways --
SECURITY.md says so and calls the seeded secrets, the self-signed TLS and the unauthenticated
admin API design rather than findings. A checker that reported those would be argued with
rather than fixed. So the rule set is SECURITY.md's IN-SCOPE list, and the sites where this
emulator's local-by-design posture legitimately produces one of those shapes are written down
with their reason instead of being silently excluded. An excluded directory teaches nobody
anything; an entry naming the host set is reviewable.
THE MEASURED BASELINE, as of the change that added sql-identifier-interpolated (R8): 93
findings across 578 non-test source files, in 85 distinct (file, rule, symbol) keys -- ALL of
them listed below, and FIFTEEN MORE that are NOT, because they were fixed in the same changes
rather than recorded. The file count is restated from a measured run: the prose here claimed
576 while the gate was printing 577, and 578 is that plus python/spark_agent/sqlident.py.
THE FIRST of those eight is why this file exists. internal/akv set InsecureSkipVerify on the
whole transport from FABRIC_ENTRA_TLS_INSECURE (docker-compose.yml sets it true;
docs/04-configuration.md documents it as being for entra-emulator's cert), on the one client
whose allowlist deliberately admits a real *.vault.azure.net -- so a secret could be fetched
from a real vault over a connection nobody authenticated, while the https requirement
checkVaultURI enforces for exactly that reason still passed. internal/server compounded it by
handing that client the transport built for the Entra JWKS fetch. The skip is now scoped to the
configured emulator vault host (akv.hostScopedTLS) and AKV builds its own transport, which is
why the akv entry below can name ONE host instead of every Azure vault domain.
SIX MORE WERE THE SAME DEFECT IN PYTHON, and they were invisible until R1 learned the stdlib
spelling of a verification skip. The rule matched requests' `verify=False` and not
`verify_mode = ssl.CERT_NONE` / `check_hostname = False`, which is the pair this repository's
own Python actually writes -- so 39 sites were unexamined, and six of them carried a credential
over the unverified connection. eventstream_kafka._fabric_request is the sharp one: it sends a
bearer token to a FABRIC_API_URL that DEFAULTS to api.fabric.microsoft.com, so the default
configuration talked to a real Microsoft endpoint with the trust check off. Four more POST
ENTRA_CLIENT_SECRET (eventstream_kafka._fabric_token, storage._mint,
storage._forge_attributed, usercontext.caller_token) and the sixth is fabric_target's
_EmulatorCredential.get_token. Each was applied to a CALL rather than to a host; all six are
now scoped per host by python/spark_agent/tls_scope.py and fabric_target's own _tls_context,
both of which cite akv.hostScopedTLS because they are the same repair one language over.
THE LAST TWO were unchecked archive extractions in e2e/azcopy/run.py -- an archive downloaded
from an aka.ms redirect, unpacked with bare extractall in both the zip and the tar branch, so
one `../../` member would have written outside WORK (on CI, the checkout). Repaired with
filter="data" on the tar and a validated members= list on the zip, which is why
archive-extraction-unchecked ships at zero rather than with two entries below.
TWO ENTRIES BELOW RECORD A FIX RATHER THAN AN ALLOWANCE, and they are the two host-scoped
helpers themselves (tls_scope.tls_context and fabric_target._tls_context). The checker sees the
two assignments that build the unverified context and cannot see the host guard above them, so
the sites still match. Their `hosts` field names what the guard actually admits, which is the

whole point: loopback/link-local/private ADDRESSES, *.localhost, *.internal, host.docker.internal and bare compose service names, and nothing else -- a public host verifies whether it is spelled as a name or as an IPv6 literal, which took a repair and a host table over both copies to be true rather than merely claimed.
R8, sql-identifier-interpolated, IS THE NEWEST AND ITS LEDGER READS DIFFERENTLY FROM THE REST.
A name spliced into SQL text is SQL SYNTAX, not a value: backticks around it look like quoting
and are not, because a backtick inside the name closes the pair and the rest is parsed. The
measured asymmetry is the whole story. The GO side of this tree was already correct everywhere
-- internal/tds.principalName doubles `]` -> `]]`, quotedID doubles `'` -> `''`,
internal/server's sqlIdent/sqlLiteral are the same pair one package over, and enterDelegated
leans on SQL Server's own QUOTENAME -- while the PYTHON side doubled not one backtick anywhere
in python/spark_agent, including onelake_security.apply, which installs the temp view that
ENFORCES OneLake row- and column-level security. A lakehouse table is a FOLDER under Tables/
created by whoever can write to OneLake, and nothing in internal/onelake rejects a backtick in
a path segment, so that name is data the whole way round: folder -> catalog.register -> SHOW
TABLES -> the view that decides which rows a principal sees.
SO THE SEVEN PYTHON SYMBOLS WERE FIXED and the SIX GO SYMBOLS ARE RECORDED, and the six entries
below say 'this is right and must stay right' rather than 'this is allowed'. The reason they are
recorded at all is a stated limit of the rule: its Go half is regex and brace-scanning rather
than a parser, so it reads the enclosing FUNCTION and cannot see the escape sitting in the
argument list, where its Python half can. The Python half DOES recognise the escape, which is
what makes the repaired sites report clean -- and that matters more than it sounds. Had escaped
sites gone on reporting, each would have needed an entry here, and then deleting the
quote_ident call would have left that entry valid and the build green: a guard that has stopped
guarding and still reports success. Removing an escape now takes `--strict` to exit 1.
`values` IS REQUIRED ON EVERY R8 ENTRY, and is to this rule what `hosts` is to R1: what decides
whether spliced SQL is safe is WHAT is interpolated and WHAT escapes it, so an entry that names
neither records the site without recording the thing worth reviewing. For the six Go entries it
is the only place the escape is written down at all. The thirteen e2e and example entries are
there because every value they interpolate is one that file itself wrote -- a module constant, a
literal in the loop it iterates -- which sits exactly ONE dataflow step past the rule's
constant narrowing; following that step is taint analysis, which this rule does not do, so they
are recorded rather than narrowed away, and a probe that starts interpolating a name from the
catalog becomes a finding again.
ONE R8 ENTRY IS NEITHER A GUARD NOR A HARNESS: onelake_security.apply, which splices the policy
author's OWN row filter as the view's source. That is the feature -- rewriting user SQL would
mean parsing it, and the module's docstring notes that a parser 95% right is a security control
5% absent -- so the splice is recorded the way python-shell-injection records the places this
repo executes submitted code. Its entry also names the limitation it creates: the ledger key is
(file, rule, symbol), so once that symbol is recorded for `sql` the gate can no longer tell an
escaped `name` from a raw one there. Verified, not assumed. For that one symbol the guard is
python/tests/test_spark_agent_sql_ident.py, which pins the emitted statement text.
Three rules ship with a zero baseline and are pure regression guards, so they appear nowhere
below: weak-random-for-secrets (no non-test Go file imports math/rand at all),
secret-compared-directly (this repo imports neither hmac.Equal nor subtle.ConstantTimeCompare;
internal/awssig is crypto/hmac's only user, for signing), and archive-extraction-unchecked --
whose Python half reached zero by the two azcopy repairs above, and whose Go half has never had
a finding to report because no non-test Go file here imports archive/zip or archive/tar.
`hosts` is required on every tls-verification-off entry and is the field that makes the entry
worth reading: it is precisely what was missing when akv's skip reached an Azure domain. It is
not an exemption on its own -- the `why` is.

hosts: the emulator's OWN listener: 127.0.0.1 or the -addr host:port it was started with
accepted.why: The `healthcheck` subcommand probes this process's own /health over the address it was told to listen on, and falls back to plain HTTP when TLS is off. The cert it must accept is the one this binary generated for itself (internal/tlscert), so there is no third party to authenticate and no credential on the request -- it sends no Authorization header at all.

hosts: cfg.EntraJWKSURL -- entra-emulator on the compose network, or a real Entra tenant when -entra-jwks-url names one
accepted.why: Fetches the JWKS to VERIFY tokens; it sends no credential. The flag is FABRIC_ENTRA_TLS_INSECURE, documented for entra-emulator's self-signed cert. Worth knowing the limit: a substituted JWKS would let an attacker mint tokens this emulator accepts, which is a local-trust decision the operator makes by setting the flag, and is why it defaults to false.

hosts: the origin derived from cfg.EntraIssuer (entra.OriginFromIssuer) -- entra-emulator's admin API
accepted.why: Workspace-identity provisioning drives entra-emulator's admin API at the issuer's origin. Same host and same flag as the JWKS fetch above, which is why it shares that trust decision rather than making a second one.

hosts: cfg.ARMURL -- arm-emulator, a compose sibling; the feed is off unless it is set
accepted.why: Reads the ARM capacities feed from arm-emulator's self-signed endpoint. The client is constructed only when FABRIC_ARM_URL names a host, so an unconfigured emulator has no such client at all.

hosts: cfg.DatabricksURL -- databricks-emulator, a compose sibling
accepted.why: Its OWN flag, FABRIC_DATABRICKS_TLS_INSECURE, rather than the Entra one: the Databricks relay is a different host with a different cert, and the two decisions are taken separately on purpose. Carries cfg.DatabricksToken, so the host set matters -- it is one configured URL and never a vendor domain this code composes itself.

hosts: cfg.AKVVaultHost ALONE -- the family's keyvault-emulator. Every AzureVaultSuffixes domain verifies whatever the flag says.
accepted.why: Scoped, and the reason this rule requires a host set. akv.hostScopedTLS routes per request host, so the skip reaches only the one configured emulator vault and a real *.vault.azure.net is always verified -- which is what makes the flag safe to leave set in a compose file that also resolves real AKV references. Before that it was transport-wide; see this file's _comment.

hosts: $ENTRA -- entra-emulator's token endpoint
accepted.why: Mints a client-credentials token against entra-emulator over its self-signed cert. The client secret it sends is the SEEDED one this repo publishes on purpose (SECURITY.md: seeded secrets are design, not a finding), and the endpoint is a compose sibling.

hosts: $FABRIC -- the emulator's own OneLake endpoint on localhost
accepted.why: Microsoft's real azure-storage-blob SDK is pointed at the emulator's OneLake surface; connection_verify=False is how the SDK is told to accept the local dev cert. The emulator family serves a self-signed cert on a compose network / localhost, and docs/05-tls-and-hosts.md documents installing the local CA as optional. Harness code, run against containers this repo starts.

RUNNING SUBMITTED CODE IS WHAT THIS COMPONENT IS FOR. SECURITY.md scopes the in-scope case precisely -- escape 'beyond the documented execution surface' -- and a notebook cell reaching the interpreter IS that surface: real Fabric runs the cell too. Recorded rather than excluded so the SET of places this repo executes arbitrary code stays enumerated, and a new exec anywhere else fails the build.

A recording or coverage directory widened so the emulator container can write a bind mount. The published image is distroless NONROOT (uid 65532) and a bind mount keeps the HOST's ownership, so a directory created by the checkout user is not writable by the container -- and Go's coverage runtime says nothing about that, leaving an empty directory that reads as 'the e2e exercised nothing' rather than 'the e2e could not say'. Docker Desktop on macOS ignores the uid mismatch, so this passes on a laptop and fails only on Linux CI; see scripts/coverage_prepare.sh and e2e/engine-matrix/run.py's ensure_out_writable for the same fix with the same comment. Harness code that ships in no artifact, on a directory holding recorded HTTP responses and coverage counters.

DELIBERATE, and the line above it says so: the terminal pane's token is printed to this process's stdout for the operator to copy into the pane, the way Jupyter prints its own. The portal is unauthenticated, so an ENDPOINT handing the token out would be equivalent to having no token -- stdout on the operator's own terminal is the narrowest channel that still works. The value is generated per run by this process, is not a cloud credential, and reaches no log file, event or error body.

hosts: the emulator's own /_emulator/clock, derived from AZURE_STORAGE_ENDPOINT -- fabric-emulator on the compose network
accepted.why: Reads the emulator's clock offset so the token-refresh deadline can follow an advanced clock. It sends NO credential at all and its failure path is `return 0`, so the worst a substituted answer buys is a refresh schedule computed from a wrong offset. The endpoint is derived from the storage endpoint this container was already given, which in this image is always the compose sibling.

hosts: $ENTRA_TOKEN_URL -- entra-emulator on the compose network
accepted.why: Mints the Storage-audience token for Sail against entra-emulator over its self-signed cert, and the comment above it has said so since it was written. This is the container ENTRYPOINT of docker/sail: it runs only inside the compose network this repo defines, where ENTRA_TOKEN_URL is set by docker-compose.yml to the sibling service. The client secret it sends is the SEEDED one this repo publishes on purpose (SECURITY.md: seeded secrets are design, not a finding). Worth naming the limit: unlike the agent's mints one directory over -- which this change host-scoped onto spark_agent/tls_scope.py -- this one is not scoped, because an image entrypoint has no non-compose caller to protect. If that ever stops being true, tls_scope is the fix.

hosts: the emulator's own portal on localhost, started by this demo script
accepted.why: A documentation demo that boots the stack and waits for the portal to answer before driving it. Sends no credential on the readiness poll, talks only to the listener it started, and ships in no artifact.

hosts: 127.0.0.1 / localhost on the ports this harness itself starts (entra-emulator, fabric-emulator and whichever sidecars the suite needs) -- never a host named by configuration
accepted.why: Harness code polling the health endpoint of a process THIS SCRIPT just started on loopback, before any credential exists. The emulator family serves a self-signed cert on a compose network / localhost, and docs/05-tls-and-hosts.md documents installing the local CA as optional. The context is built inline for the readiness poll and reaches nothing else; a harness that cannot reach its own listener has nothing to test.

hosts: loopback, link-local and private ADDRESSES, plus *.localhost, *.internal, host.docker.internal and bare compose service names ALONE -- the emulator entra at ENTRA_EMULATOR_URL / ENTRA_URL. Any PUBLIC host named there returns None and is fully verified, including a global-unicast IPv6 literal: an address is decided on the parsed address, not on whether it contains a dot.
accepted.why: THE HOST-SCOPED HELPER ITSELF, and the one entry here that records a fix rather than an allowance. The unverified context this builds is returned ONLY for a host that parses as a loopback, link-local or private ADDRESS, or is `.localhost`, `.internal`, `host.docker.internal` or a bare compose service name; every other host -- including every real Microsoft domain, named or spelled as an IPv6 literal -- gets `None`, which urllib reads as full default verification. The address branch is a REPAIR: the first version decided on `'.' not in host`, which read every IPv6 literal as local because no IPv6 address contains a dot, and on `startswith('127.')`, which is a prefix test against a NAME and so admitted the attacker-chosen `127.0.0.1.evil.com`. Both halves are now pinned by a host table over BOTH copies (python/tests/test_spark_agent_tls_scope.py) -- a security boundary nothing asserted is exactly the failure this ledger's siblings are written about. The checker sees the two assignments and cannot see the guard above them, which is why this is recorded instead of being invisible. It is the same shape as internal/akv's hostScopedTLS, and it is what replaced six unconditional skips in this change. fabric-target is a separate distributable and cannot import spark_agent's copy, which is why the helper is duplicated rather than shared. It guards _EmulatorCredential.get_token, which POSTs a client secret.

accepted.values: TWO values with deliberately OPPOSITE treatment, which is the whole reason this entry exists. `name` is DATA -- a OneLake `Tables/` folder name, created by whoever can write there and arriving here via catalog registration and SHOW TABLES -- and is escaped with `sqlident.quote_ident`, which doubles the backtick. `sql` is `secure_view_sql`'s output and is spliced RAW, because its relation half is the policy author's OWN row filter: the module's docstring explains that rewriting user SQL would mean parsing it, and 'a parser that is 95% right is a security control that is 5% absent', so the filter is used as the view's source instead. Column names in that projection come from the same policy.
accepted.why: SPLICING AUTHOR-WRITTEN POLICY SQL IS THE FEATURE; splicing a NAME was the defect, and the name half is fixed rather than recorded. A OneLake row filter IS SQL text by design -- the principalAccess API returns it as text precisely so a third-party engine can apply it, which is what this module does on Fabric's behalf -- so there is no version of this that does not place author SQL into a statement. The entry is here so the set of places this repository splices policy SQL stays enumerated, exactly as python-shell-injection records the set of places it executes submitted code. The identifier it sits beside is escaped, and R8 would report this symbol again if that stopped being true. AND THE LIMITATION THIS ENTRY CREATES, stated because it is not obvious and it is the reason the test table exists: the ledger key is (file, rule, symbol), so once this symbol is recorded for the `sql` splice the checker can no longer tell `quote_ident(name)` from a raw `{name}` here -- both are the same finding under the same key, and both report green. Verified rather than assumed: reverting the name to raw leaves `--strict` at exit 0. So for THIS symbol the guard is not the gate but python/tests/test_spark_agent_sql_ident.py, which pins the emitted CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP VIEW text and fails on exactly that revert. Every other repaired site in spark_agent is NOT ledgered and is therefore held by the gate itself: removing an escape there is an unrecorded finding and exit 1.
